etymology: Hebrew tsaphon, “north” or “hidden place,” a town in the valley of the Jordan given to the tribe of Gad east of the river.
biblical_def: Zaphon was a town in the Jordan valley assigned to the tribe of Gad when Moses and Joshua portioned out the land east of the river. It lay among the cities that had belonged to Sihon king of Heshbon, and it is named with Beth-aram, Beth-nimrah, and Succoth as the inheritance of Gad along the river up to the edge of the sea of Chinnereth (Jos 13:27). Some have read the gathering of the men of Ephraim against Jephthah, who “went northward” (Jdg 12:1), as a passing over unto Zaphon, where envy and pride nearly kindled a civil war among the tribes. The dictionary does not labour the obscure points of its geography; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this little valley town among the goodly heritage He measured out to His people. The lines were fallen unto Gad in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were not the work of chance or of the sword alone, but of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Zaphon stands as a witness that no portion of the saint’s heritage is too small for the care of Him who apportioned it.
webster_summary: A town of the Jordan valley given to the tribe of Gad, named among the cities of the kingdom of Sihon.

corruption_paragraphs: Zaphon is a town of the sacred geography, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name in the apportioning of Gad may know it for a real place in a real inheritance, given by a real God to a real people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of providence over the bounds of habitation. He who set the borders of Gad by the river and the sea is the same who has determined the times before appointed and the bounds of every nation and every soul. The saint who feels his portion small or hidden may remember Zaphon, a name barely spoken in Scripture, yet written for ever in the book of God’s faithful dividing of the land.

etymology: Hebrew Abel hash-Shittim, “meadow of the acacias,” the last encampment of Israel in the plains of Moab before the crossing of Jordan.
biblical_def: Abel-shittim, called also simply Shittim, was the last camp of Israel in the plains of Moab, by the Jordan over against Jericho, before the nation passed over into the promised land. From Beth-jeshimoth unto Abel-shittim the tents of the tribes were spread along the river (Num 33:49). It was a place of both temptation and triumph. Here Israel, at the very border of the inheritance, was drawn into whoredom with the daughters of Moab and bowed down to Baal-peor, and the plague consumed twenty and four thousand until Phinehas rose up and turned away the wrath of God (Num 25:1). Here too the second numbering of the people was taken, and from here Joshua sent the two spies into Jericho. The prophet Micah bids Israel remember the way from Shittim unto Gilgal, that they may know the righteousness of the LORD (Mic 6:5). The dictionary holds up Abel-shittim as the meadow where the flesh was proved at the threshold of promise. These things were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come (1Co 10:11); the believer nearest his rest is not beyond the reach of temptation, and must watch unto prayer until Jordan is crossed indeed.

Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall; the meadow of the acacias is a standing warning that nearness to promise is no charter for carelessness of soul.

etymology: Hebrew Qiryathayim, “double city” or “twin towns,” spelled Kirjathaim in the Authorized Version, a town of Reuben east of the Jordan.
biblical_def: Kiriathaim was a town east of the Jordan, built up by the children of Reuben among the cities they took from Sihon and apportioned for their inheritance (Num 32:37; Jos 13:19). Its name, “double city,” marks it as a place of some size and strength in the tableland of Moab. Yet the later history of Kiriathaim is a history of judgment, for when Reuben grew weak and the land passed again into the hand of Moab, the town became a stronghold of the idolaters. The prophets named it in their oracles against Moab: Kiriathaim is confounded and taken (Jer 48:1), and the LORD declared He would open the side of Moab from his cities, the glory of the country, naming Beth-jeshimoth, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim (Eze 25:9). The dictionary marks the town as a witness to the perishable nature of an inheritance not held in faith. What Reuben built and did not keep, Moab seized and lost in turn under the judgment of God. The double city was no surer for its double name; the strength of a place is not in its walls but in the favour of the LORD, and where He withdraws, the strongest city is confounded.

Reuben built Kiriathaim and lost it; Moab held it and was confounded. Where the LORD withdraws His keeping, the double city is no surer than the single, and the lesson stands that nothing is safe which is not safe in Him.

etymology: Hebrew Sibmah, perhaps “coolness” or “fragrance,” a town of Reuben east of the Jordan, famous for its vineyards.
biblical_def: Sibmah was a town of Reuben in the tableland east of the Jordan, built among the cities taken from Sihon (Num 32:38; Jos 13:19). It was renowned above its neighbours for the richness of its vines, so that the prophets, lamenting the fall of Moab, took up the vine of Sibmah as the very emblem of a fruitfulness laid waste. Isaiah cried, I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah: I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for the shouting for thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen (Isa 16:9). Jeremiah took up the same lament, weeping for the vine of Sibmah whose plants were gone over the sea, for the spoiler had fallen upon her summer fruits and her vintage (Jer 48:32). The dictionary marks Sibmah as the vineyard of false security. Her branches stretched far and her fruit was abundant, but the lords of the heathen broke down her principal plants, and her shouting harvest fell silent under the judgment of God. The richest vine is no defence against the wrath of heaven, and the joy of the harvest is turned to wailing where the people forget the Giver of the increase.

etymology: Hebrew Mephaath, perhaps “height” or “splendour,” a Levitical city in the territory of Reuben east of the Jordan.
biblical_def: Mephaath was a city in the allotment of Reuben, on the tableland east of the Jordan, set apart with its suburbs for the Levites of the family of Merari (Jos 13:18; Jos 21:37; 1Ch 6:79). It belonged to no field of its own, for Levi received no portion of land among his brethren; the LORD was their inheritance, and they dwelt scattered through the tribes in forty and eight cities, that the knowledge of the law might be spread among all Israel. Mephaath was one of these, a small priestly outpost on the eastern frontier. In the latter days, when Moab seized the eastern tableland, Mephaath came under the prophet’s word of judgment, for judgment was come upon the plain country, upon Holon, and upon Jahazah, and upon Mephaath (Jer 48:21). The dictionary marks the town as a Levitical city, a place that taught the doctrine of the priestly tribe whose treasure was not in lands but in the service of God. The Levite at Mephaath held no estate of his own, yet he held the better portion; for the LORD Himself was the lot of his inheritance and his cup, and the man whose portion is God is richer in a borrowed city than the Moabite in all his fields.

etymology: Hebrew Gath-Rimmon, “winepress of the pomegranate,” the name of two Levitical cities, one in Dan and one in the half-tribe of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Gath-rimmon, “the winepress of the pomegranate,” was the name of two Levitical cities given to the Kohathites among the suburbs of the tribes. The first lay in the territory of Dan, named with Jehud and Bene-berak in the coastal plain (Jos 19:45), and was set apart with its suburbs for the Levites (Jos 21:24). The second was in the half-tribe of Manasseh west of the Jordan, likewise given to the Kohathites with its suburbs (Jos 21:25; 1Ch 6:69). The two towns of one name witness, like all the Levitical cities, to the wisdom of God in scattering the priestly tribe through the inheritance of Israel. Levi was divided in Jacob and dispersed in Israel, yet the curse pronounced upon his father’s cruelty was turned by grace into a blessing, for the dispersion of Levi became the means by which the law and the worship of God were carried into every quarter of the land. The dictionary marks Gath-rimmon as one of these priestly outposts. The winepress of the pomegranate yielded, in the providence of God, not wine alone but the sweeter fruit of the knowledge of His statutes among His people.

etymology: Hebrew Eltheqeh, perhaps “let God spew out” or “God is its fear,” a Levitical city in the territory of Dan.
biblical_def: Eltekeh was a city in the allotment of the tribe of Dan, named with Gibbethon and Baalath in the lists of the conquest (Jos 19:44). It was afterward set apart, with Gibbethon, as a Levitical city given out of the tribe of Dan to the Kohathites, with its suburbs for their cattle (Jos 21:23). Thus Eltekeh, like Mephaath and Gath-rimmon, was a priestly outpost, a place where the Levite dwelt without a field of his own that the law of God might be near to the men of Dan. The Levitical cities were appointed of the LORD through Moses, and among them were the six cities of refuge to which the manslayer might flee (Num 35:6); so the priestly towns were not only seats of teaching but sanctuaries of mercy, where the avenger of blood was stayed and judgment tempered with grace. The dictionary marks Eltekeh as one such city. Its name, by one reading, sounds the very fear of God that the Levite was sent to teach; and the town stands for the truth that wherever the ministry of the word is planted, there the knowledge and the fear of the LORD are carried among the people, and there mercy has a dwelling-place.

etymology: Hebrew Baalath, “mistress” or “lady,” the feminine of Baal, a town of Dan afterward fortified by Solomon.
biblical_def: Baalath was a town in the allotment of Dan, named with Eltekeh and Gibbethon among the cities of the tribe (Jos 19:44). In the days of the kingdom it was rebuilt and fortified by Solomon, who is recorded to have built Baalath, and Tadmor in the wilderness, among the store cities and chariot cities of his dominion (1Ki 9:18; 2Ch 8:6). The name of the town carries within it the feminine form of Baal, a lingering trace of the old Canaanite worship of the land before Israel came. The dictionary does not pass over so plain a thing. Israel was commanded to destroy the names of the false gods out of the land, and the LORD promised by Hosea that He would take away the names of Baalim out of the mouth of His people, that they should no more be remembered by their name (Hos 2:17). That a city of Israel still bore a name compounded with Baal is a quiet witness to how deeply the idolatry of Canaan was rooted, and how slow and incomplete was its purging. Baalath stands for the half-cleansed inheritance, where the works of the people stood beside the names of the old gods, and the call to a thorough reformation went long unanswered.

The town is recorded that the reader may mark how a name outlasts the worship that bore it.

Israel was to blot out the names of the false gods, yet a city of the inheritance still bore the name of Baal in the days of Solomon. etymology: Hebrew Shaalbim, “place of foxes,” spelled Shaalabbin in Joshua, a town in the allotment of Dan.
biblical_def: Shaalbim was a town in the inheritance of Dan, lying near Aijalon in the lowland (Jos 19:42, where the Authorized Version spells it Shaalabbin). It is chiefly remembered for the report of the unfinished conquest, for the Amorites would dwell in mount Heres in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, refusing to be driven out, until the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed and made them tributaries (Jdg 1:35). In the days of Solomon the town fell within the district of one of his officers, the son of Dekar (1Ki 4:9). The dictionary marks Shaalbim as a town of incomplete obedience. The LORD had commanded Israel to dispossess the inhabitants of the land utterly, yet here, as in many places, the Canaanite was suffered to remain, set to tribute rather than driven out. And the word of the LORD by the angel was fulfilled, that the nations spared should be as thorns in their sides, and their gods a snare unto them (Jdg 2:3). Shaalbim, the place of foxes, became a parable of the small compromises that nest in the inheritance of the saints; what is not driven out wholly will return to vex and to ensnare, and partial obedience is the seed of later sorrow.
webster_summary: A town of Dan where the Amorites long remained, a witness to Israel’s incomplete conquest.

corruption_paragraphs: Shaalbim has met no redefinition from the present age, surviving as a name in the record of the unfinished conquest. The dictionary records it that the reader may understand why the Canaanite was suffered to remain, and what that sparing cost.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of incomplete obedience. The Amorite at Shaalbim was set to tribute but not driven out, and the spared nations became thorns and snares to Israel. So the believer is warned that the small compromises he suffers to nest in his heart will return to vex and ensnare him. What is not put off wholly will rise again, and partial obedience is the seed of later sorrow.

etymology: Hebrew Ir-Shemesh, “city of the sun,” a town in the allotment of Dan, akin to Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun.”
biblical_def: Ir-shemesh, “the city of the sun,” was a town named in the borders of the inheritance of Dan, set down with Zorah and Eshtaol as the coast of their portion (Jos 19:41). Its name, like that of the neighbouring Beth-shemesh, bears witness to the worship of the sun that the heathen of Canaan practised before Israel possessed the land. The dictionary does not pass the name by, for the Scripture itself warns against the very thing it remembers. Moses charged Israel that they should not lift up their eyes unto heaven, and when they saw the sun, and the moon, and the stars, be driven to worship and serve them, which the LORD had divided unto all nations (Deu 4:19). Israel was to worship not the sun but the Maker of the sun, whose heavens declare His glory (Psa 19:1). And the prophet Malachi turned the very figure to Christ, promising that unto them that fear God’s name the Sun of righteousness should arise with healing in His wings (Mal 4:2). So Ir-shemesh, a city named for the created light, points beyond itself to the uncreated Light, and reproves the folly of bowing to the lamp while forgetting the Lord who lit it.
webster_summary: A town of Dan whose name, “city of the sun,” recalls the sun-worship of Canaan and reproves it.

The Sun of righteousness, who is Christ, is the true Light the name foreshadows.

corruption_summary: A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; its name reproves the worship of the creature in place of the Creator.
corruption_paragraphs: Ir-shemesh has met no redefinition from the present age, but its name preserves the memory of a corruption the Scripture itself condemns, the worship of the sun and the host of heaven. The dictionary records the town that the reader may see how the names of the land bore witness to its old idolatry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the creature is never to be worshipped in the place of the Creator. The city of the sun is a standing reproof to the folly that bows to the lamp and forgets the Lord who lit it. The heavens declare His glory, but they are not Himself; and the true Light is the Sun of righteousness, who arises with healing for them that fear the name of God.
